title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
summary: You get a string `s`. Find the longest substring of `s` in which no character appears more than once, and return its length. A substring is a run of neighboring characters, so it can't skip any. Every character counts, including spaces, digits and symbols, and an empty string has an answer of `0`.

examples.explanation: "unshi" and "shine" each have five different characters. Every longer run holds a second "s" or a second "n".
Digits and symbols count as characters. "+1=2" has no repeat, but any run that holds both 1s does.

constraints: s is made of printable ASCII characters: English letters, digits, symbols and spaces

approaches.twist: Shrink from the left while the new character is already in the window.
Store each character's last index in a dict, and when it repeats inside the window, jump l just past that earlier copy.
Check every substring, growing a set from each start index, and keep the longest one without a repeat.
approaches.note: Works, but there are about n²/2 substrings to check, so it takes O(n²) time. The target is O(n).

signals.meaning: The answer is one unbroken run of characters. Grow a window on the right, and keep the longest one that follows the rule.
Keep the window's characters in a set. Checking whether the new character is already there, with the in operator, takes O(1) time.
Only 95 different characters exist, and the window never holds one twice, so a set of its characters never grows past 95 entries.

constraintReading: len(s) can reach 5·10⁴, so checking all of its substrings, about 1.25·10⁹ of them, is O(n²) and far too slow. Aim for O(n): each character should enter the window once and leave it at most once. The O(1) space target still allows a set, because the window never holds a character twice: the set can't grow past the 95 printable ASCII characters.

hints.clarify: Does a space count as a character? Yes: every character counts, including spaces, digits and symbols. Can the substring skip characters? No: it's a run of neighbors. Try "abab" by hand: "ab" and "ba" have no repeat, but any run of three holds a letter twice, so the answer is 2.
hints.approach: Sliding window. Keep a window from `l` to `r` that never holds a character twice, and a set `window` of the characters in it. Move `r` right one step at a time. If the new character is already in the set, drop characters from the left, moving `l` forward, until it's gone; then add the new one and measure the window. Each character enters the window once and leaves at most once, so one pass is enough.
hints.whyNot: Checking every substring works, but there are about n²/2 of them: over 10⁹ when `s` has 5·10⁴ characters. Restarting from each start index also reads the same characters again and again. The window keeps what it already knows: when a repeat arrives, only the part up to its first copy has to go.

slots.setup: An empty set `window` for the characters in the window, `l` at 0, and `best` at 0.
slots.loop: Move `r` through `s` from left to right. The character at `r` is the one about to join the window.
slots.update: While the character at `r` is already in `window`, remove the character at `l` from the set and move `l` one step right. Stop as soon as the repeat is gone.
slots.record: Add the character at `r` to `window`. The window from `l` to `r` now has no repeat, and its length is r − l + 1; keep the larger of that and `best`.
slots.return: Once `r` has passed the end, return `best`. An empty string never enters the loop, so it returns 0.

solution.explanation: Each character is added to `window` once, when `r` reaches it, and removed at most once, when `l` passes it, so the two pointers take at most 2n steps in total: O(n) time. The window never holds a character twice, so the set has at most 95 entries, one per printable ASCII character: O(1) extra space however long `s` is.

events.label: shrink
events.say: {s[r]!r} is already in the window, so drop {s[l]!r} from the left

events.label: new best
events.say: {s[r]!r} isn't in the window, so add it. s[{l}..{r}] has no repeat, and its length, {r - l + 1}, is the longest so far

events.label: grow
events.say: {s[r]!r} isn't in the window, so add it. s[{l}..{r}] has no repeat, but its length, {r - l + 1}, doesn't beat {best}

events.label: return
events.say: No characters are left, so return the longest length found: {best}

predict.ask: Will the next character force the window to shrink?
predict.answerWhen: r + 1 < len(s) and (s[r + 1] in window or s[r + 1] == s[r])

predict.ask: Once this character is dropped, will the window be free of repeats?

related.relation: Same grow-and-shrink window, but letters may repeat: the window breaks only when it would need more than k changes, so you keep letter counts instead of a set.
Also keeps a left end behind a right end, but the left end jumps straight to each new lowest price instead of stepping past repeats.
